# Copper June 2012 - In March we were discussing copper range bound around the $8500/t level. As the market has moved lower, in tandem with disappointing macro news, prices are now range bound around the $7500/t level. The fact that copper prices have not slipped further and appear for now to be relatively well supported in the face of a raft of broadly downbeat news, could be viewed as being quite positive for those with a bullish bent. - Largely as a result of a more negative stance towards so called “risk assets” following the latest chapter of the European debt crisis, we have altered our price profile for the second half of the year. We now expect cash prices to average $7600 in the third quarter, with deviations around this largely driven by macro news. Our forecast improvement in Chinese demand in the final part of the year should see prices move higher in Q4. The net result is a lower 2012 forecast with our average cash price now estimated at $8047/t from $8477/t previously. Changes to both demand and supply have combined to reduce our expected deficit this year to ~132kt from ~178kt previously. - Green bamboo shoots of recovery give us further conviction in our 7% consumption growth forecast for China, although changes elsewhere have led us to downgrade our estimate of global demand growth in 2012. Principally, downgrades in Western Europe and the rest of Asia are responsible for the cut to 2.7% from 3.2% previously. - The copper concentrate market is showing some signs of re-awaking following a quiet couple of months, with representative spot selling terms from miners to traders in June increased slightly to $27.5/t and 2.75c/lb. The negative arbitrage between the SHFE and LME 3 month copper prices continued to narrow, after accounting for VAT the arbitrage averaged $132/t through (SHFE under LME) to the last week of June compared with $243/t in May. However, with TCRCs remaining unfavourable Chinese spot buying activity over and above material already secured through long term contracts was still limited to ‘hand to mouth’ requirements with buying terms moving slightly higher compared with the previous month with levels in the region of $48/t & 4.8c/lb being reported. Copper Monthly Update 

## Market Developments 

**Copper’s new average closer to $7500/t than $8500/t** In March we were discussing copper range bound trade around the $8500/t level.  As the market has moved lower, in tandem with disappointing macro news, prices are now range bound around the $7500/t level.  After declining by over $1,100/t in May it was unlikely that cash and 3M quotes would come under quite such severe downward pressure this month, despite a number of negative factors over-hanging the market.  The fact that copper prices have not slipped further and appear for now to be relatively well supported in the face of a raft of broadly downbeat news could be viewed as being quite positive for those with a bullish bent. 

June started on the back foot after downbeat Chinese PMI data weighed on sentiment.  At least the UK’s Jubilee celebrations over an extra-long weekend that closed the LME for two days, gave traders a chance to catch their breath and take the opportunity to reassess conditions.  The extended break seemed to lift spirits in the base metals market, which were further buoyed by hopes that the Europeans would come up with a solution to help Greece and its well documented problems from also overwhelming Spain, while a cut in Chinese interest rates added further impetus to pull prices back up towards $7500/t from levels closer to $7300/t in the prior trading days.  However, the mood turned bearish again as market participants sought to rationalise China’s rate cut ahead of a slew of data releases, whilst Spain’s credit rating was cut and the focus switched to a second Greek election in just six weeks.  The mood turned positive again on hopes that a new round of quantitative easing in the US would soothe bruised markets, but was shortlived. 

**Grelief turns to despair as hopes for QEIII sink** The outcome of the Greek election ought to have been a major relief for financial markets, although any cheer quickly dissipated amid the realisation that the win for the pro-bailout party would mean the formation of a fragile coalition government, which will struggle to push through the required legislation. The big fear, of course, is that this simply results in “the can being kicked down the road”, rather than a swift and decisive conclusion to Greece’s problems.  Meanwhile, market participants hoping for a new round of Quantitative Easing were left twisting in the wind when the US Fed chose to expand its “Operation Twist” program instead, a less aggressive strategy to stimulate economic activity.  Throughout the remainder of the month prices continued to bump around without clear direction. 

**Back to back** In mid-May, several Chinese producers announced their intention to export material onto the LME, ostensibl

y in a noble move to ease tightness in the copper market. Copper prices did trade lower while at the same time, the cash to three months backwardation dissipated after it had flared out to as much as $135/t in May on closing prices. The contango remained in place until the latter part of June when the market flipped back into a cash to threes backwardation. Part of the explanation for the wide backwardation in May was declining LME stocks alongside a sudden and sharp rise in cancelled warrants (as traders to moved material to China ahead of an expected upturn in demand), reflecting a genuinely tight market ex China. This situation was of course exacerbated by Glencore’s requirement for material to cover lost output from its Pasar refinery in the Philippines, which had not declared _force majeure._ These factors combined to result in a dominant position emerging on the LME. This is happening now. The LME’s latest banding report indicates that one market participant is holding between 40% and 49% of available warrants and there also appears to be one dominant holder squeezing the short side of the market. #### **Copper exchange stocks and cash LME price** 900 12000

Metals Market Service Monthly Update - June 2012 Page 2 of 22 Copper Monthly Update One further similarity is the dislocation of inventory. As stocks in the US were being moved to China at the start of the year, Chinese demand was disappointing, leading to a build up of inventory on the SHFE and in bonded warehouses. Meanwhile, stocks were consistently leaving LME warehouses resulting in a tight ex China global market. Accounting for around 40% of global demand, China’s stocks ought to take a similar share of the global figure. Our estimates suggest that over half of the global copper metal inventories are being held in China, despite the recent shipments of material to nearby LME warehouses. As such, with China holding more than its fair share of copper, even in the relatively sluggish demand scenario across the rest of the world, prices have remained reasonably well supported on the LME. We forecast a deficit this year but more importantly, this will be the third consecutive year that there has been a shortfall in supply. With this in mind, it is not surprising that we are in backwardation and LME continues to trade at a premium to SHFE. **Chinese smelters close export plan early** The plan by Chinese producers to export material onto the LME resulted in a further increase in exports in May, which managed to offset a surprise upturn in imports. China shipped 102kt of refined copper in May, its largest ever single month of exports, which took the edg

e off the jump in imports, which climbed to 302kt from 273kt the prior month. The result was that net imports were at their lowest level since July of last year. As we noted above, ostensibly the exports plan was executed to ease the tightness on the LME but may also have been aimed at narrowing the arbitrage between LME and Shanghai prices. This had not only meant that imports of cathode were significantly more expensive for Chinese consumers but also that smelters, importing concentrate basis the LME and selling with reference to the SHFE, were taking a major hit. Indeed, in tandem with the decline in LME prices, the arbitrage has also narrowed significantly, with the premium to SHFE material less than $50/t on average in June compared to more than $400/t in April, basis cash prices. We understand that these price movements prompted the Chinese smelters behind the export plan to halt the programme early. #### **Shanghai/LME arbitrage ($/t) vs refined copper imports** 600 450

**Rise in Chinese premia suggests demand improvement** Whether it was the shipments out of China that served to tighten the domestic market or perhaps simply an upturn in demand, we understand that premia have moved higher over the past month. Material is now attracting premiums in the $60-$90/t range, compared to $30-$70/t a month ago. A number of factors seem to be driving this shift, not least improving domestic demand. It does appear that there was improved activity at rod mills in June as a result of a number of major energy projects starting up. Given that these projects were already planned, advancing further infrastructure investment must surely point to further improvements in demand in the second half of the year. Meanwhile, data releases in the past few weeks have also revealed an upturn in end use sectors such as air conditioners and automotive in May which should also be supportive of an upturn in orders at semis producers. Moreover, infrastructure and other purchase incentive schemes give us conviction in a second half upswing. Increased activity at semis producers should lend itself to cathode purchases to restock their supply pipeline. That said we understand there was also some speculative restocking when prices were trading at their lowest levels. Indeed, there has been a significant upturn in interest for spot cathode, for both prompt deliveries and for deliveries further out. The drawdown of stocks at both SHFE and bonded warehouses, have also supported premia higher, although we understand that some of the material has been bought by investors who have moved cathode into their own sheds. We und

erstand that a significant part of the material that is held in bonded warehouse stocks is tied up in financing deals and as such, not available to the market. As a result, bonded inventories do not need to decline too much for premia to be nudged higher. These positive signs, alongside better performance from some end use sectors, allow us to be increasingly confident in our full year forecast of a 7% expansion in Chinese consumption. **US premia surge to 7.5c/lb…** China is not the only region that is experiencing higher premia. The rise in US premia over the past few months has been particularly dramatic, with material for prompt delivery now quoted as high as 7.5c/lb, although if the need is less urgent cathode can be sourced in the range 6-7c/lb. As with China, a number of factors have combined to force up premia, but the key driver is simply a shortage of truck drivers, which is pushing up delivery costs. In addition, the delayed start up at Kennecott’s Garfield smelter and refinery following a scheduled maintenance shutdown has tightened cathode availability at a time when scrap has been in short supply. The commissioning of the 100% scrap fed SDI-LaFarga rod mill in Indiana and a build up of scrap inventories ahead of the start-up, squeezed supplies and made it difficult for some semis producers to source material, let alone at narrow discounts. As a result some semi fabricators have had to source cathode instead. It is also worth pointing out that given COMEX is trading at a discount to the LME, premiums that are based on COMEX prices need to be sufficiently high to make up for this discount and thus enable traders to turn a profit. Meanwhile, in Western Europe, material is changing hands at similar levels to last month of around $80/t as interest is soft ahead of the summer and even as European exchange stocks continue to ebb lower. **..as exchange stocks move lower overall** In the context of rising premia it comes as no surprise that total exchange stocks have been moving lower overall, despite an increase on the LME. The rise in LME stocks has been concentrated in Asia, the result of Chinese shipments to nearby warehouses, although this has been tempered by modest declines in Europe and the US. As such, the 100kt or so of Chinese exports has certainly not translated into a 100kt rise in LME stocks. Rather, since the plan was announced at the end of April, total stocks on the LME have risen by little more than 13kt as a c.75kt increase in copper at A

sian warehouses was offset by 40kt of shipments out of US locations and a decline of c.22kt in Europe.  At the time of writing total LME stocks stand at 255kt, up from 231kt at the end of May.  In Shanghai inventories have slipped further, down to 130kt from 157kt a month ago, while material in COMEX warehouses has eased to 49kt from 54kt last month. 

**Full year price forecast dragged lower by European debt woes** Largely as a result of a more negative stance towards so called “risk assets” following the latest chapter of the European debt crisis, we have altered our price profile for the second half of the year.  We now expect cash prices to average $7600 in the third quarter, with deviations around this largely driven by macro news.  Our forecast improvement in Chinese demand in the final part of the year should see prices move higher in Q4.  The net result is a lower 2012 forecast with our average cash price now estimated at $8047/t from $8477/t previously.  Changes to both demand and supply have combined to reduce our expected deficit this year to ~132kt from ~178 previously. 

Copper is one of the few base metals that is currently trading comfortably above its marginal cost of production, although a sense of nervousness does seem to have enveloped copper miners over the past few months, in the wake of lower prices.  This is not manifesting itself in production cut backs but there does seem to be an increasingly cautious tone towards plans for future growth.  Thus far, there have not been any announcements of cancelled projects, although various companies have hinted at re-evaluating their plans.  One recent example is Xstrata’s announcement of its intention to sell its majority stake in its Frieda River project in Papua New Guinea.  Given Xstrata’s fairly long list of projects, it is perhaps not surprising that this is one that could be sacrificed given that it is a relatively difficult project based on its location.  One other aspect is of course that Glencore’s copper assets tend to be in high risk locations, so it could have been felt that to balance the overall risk profile of the combined group it would be better to offload some, or all of Frieda River.

However, the key factors driving producers to re-evaulate their projects in the current ‘lower price’ environment are ongoing capital expenditure cost escalation and availability of finance.  The chart below is from the Wood Mackenzie Copper Mine Cost Service and converts disclosed capex revisions, excluding scope changes, into annual equivalent escalation rates.  The chart reveals that even in the depths of the financial crisis, costs were escalating at double-digit rates and have moved higher since then.  In 2011, for example, Wood Mackenzie noted 15 capex revisions with an average escalation rate of 28% over 2010.  This is significant because an increase in costs could make a marginal proje

ct uneconomic and it could therefore be either cancelled or deferred. This would have implications for our market balances beyond the remit of this monthly report. It must be noted, however, that today’s copper price is still above our long term incentive price of $3/lb. #### **Copper mine capital expenditure escalation (%)** 40%

For the larger companies financing is unlikely to be the major stumbling block as many projects will be self financed through their own cash flow or debt facilities that are already in place. However, for smaller companies, the recapitalisation of banks and a generally lower appetite for risk could make it increasingly difficult to get financing for projects. A further problem related to bringing on future mine supply, although not directly related to either of the above factors, is the availability of power. In Chile, for example, it is becoming increasingly difficult for power plants to obtain the requisite environmental permits for projects to go ahead, with Endesa’s 740MW Punta Alcalde thermoelectric project the latest casualty. The power shortage is particularly acute in the north of Chile, where most of the country’s copper mines and mine projects are situated. The problem is further exacerbated by the fact that Chile has two power grids, the SING in the north and the SIC in the central southern regions. There has been discussion of linking the two grids for years and this may help even out Chile's demand profile and reduce the need for some new power generation but linking the grids is expensive. The key danger is that there is not sufficient power to be able to meet the needs of future mining projects, which in some cases are likely to be more energy intensive in any case because of the need for desalination plants and the need to pump water. The high altitude of some of these mines results in water needing to be pumped up hill which becomes exponentially more costly the longer and steeper the distance of the pipes. Although the factors that we outline above do not form the base case of our mine production forecasts they do underscore continued difficulties that the copper market faces in bringing new capacity on stream. ## Consumption 

This month we focus on some positive structural developments in consumption in the United States and Brazil.  After a period of gloom both markets are now starting to benefit from new investments in wire rod, brass mill and wire and cable capacity that should be favourable for future local demand prospects. One can doubt if the scale of the investments is fully justified given the economic and end use market outlook, but nevertheless the projects are being planned and commissioned.  In Europe it seems that the long overdue rationalisation of the brass mill industry may be coming a step closer.  While in Taiwan the semis and wire and cable industry has recovered quickly from a poor start to the year.  We believe this a prelude to much brighter prospects there and in Mainland China in the second half of 2012. 

### **The United States** 

**SDI La Farga enters production…** In mid-June SDI La Farga’s rod mill commissioned in New Haven, IN.  The 180 million lbs (81,600t/a) capacity mill occupies an 85,000 square foot facility and represents an investment of US$39m. SDI selected the New Haven site near Fort Wayne due to the proximity of OmniSource’s midwest non ferrous scrap processing facilities, the good nearby highway links and because the mill’s target customers are within a 400-500 mile shipping radius.  OmniSource will be the 55/45 joint venture’s primary supplier of scrap copper while La Farga, through its technology partner Continuus Properzi, is providing the plant that will process No.2 birch cliff copper scrap into 8mm wire rod.  OmniSource’s stockpiling ahead of production has contributed to a slight narrowing of the discount of No.2 scrap to Comex which was quoted at 35-38c/lb recently compared to 40-45c/lb in March. 

**…and vies with Chinese buyers** The view from one unnamed buyer from a US wire and cable company on the new mill was that, “They are looking for the big spread between cathode and scrap to make it viable, and I think it’s going to disappear”.  How

ever, Russ Rinn, President and CEO of OmniSource countered, “What we are going to be consuming is a blip on the radar as far as the Chinese are concerned”.   A scrap trader, commenting on the likely market scenario said, “They are a big company, but they are not as big as that whole country.  When China comes in, they’re coming in to buy, and SDI will have to react.”  Wood Mackenzie considers that SDI La Farga is certain to capture some market share from existing US rod mills serving the open market and that this could displace some refined consumption depending on how rapidly SDI La Farga are able to ramp up their production.  A more uncertain question is to what extent will rod and drawn wire exporters to US be disadvantaged.  Imports currently fulfil around 10% of US rod consumption needs.  80% of this comes from Canada (chiefly from Nexans’ Montreal mill), 8% each from Turkey and Mexico and the balance of 4% from diverse sources. 

**Tube mill investments on their way** Although Golden Dragon’s investment plans for commercial tube production in Thomasville-West Wilcox industrial park, Alabama, have attracted most publicity recently other projects have been moving ahead more quickly.  Cambridge-Lee Industries broke ground on its 195,000 square foot commercial tube facility at Reading, PA, in May with completion planned for May 2013.  Cambridge-Lee has long manufactured plumbing tube from this site but the new investment will add thin wall inner grooved ACR tube to the product range.  The equipment for the expansion will come from IUSA’s US$100 million Eagle Copper Tube mill project which was discontinued in Laredo, TX, in late 2007.  It is hoped the expansion will add up to 250 jobs to the 300 already employed at Reading. 

**Golden Dragon’s 60,000t/a tube mill slated for 2013** The company has settled on a new site in Wilcox County after the original site in Thomasville was considered to be too small to meet future expansion needs.  Tree clearing work has already begun on the site and Golden Dragon will take ownership of 140 acres in the coming weeks.  Construction will take 18-24 months and will eventually create 300-500 permanent jobs.  State tax incentives, proximity to a rail line and access to the Port of Mobile each played a role in the final selection of the location.  But opinions are strongly divided on the project.  In the quest to provide much needed manufacturing jobs, local officials could argue that “Now is a very good time for China to invest.  This is very similar to what Japan did (in America) 20-30 years ago”.  Countervailing antidumping petitioners Cerro Flow Products, Wieland Copper Products and Mueller Copper Tube Company would rightly disagree citing the substantial investments that each has made in their own US tube mills to raise productivity and to safeguard existing US manufacturing jobs. 

**But do the tube market projections really add up?** According to preliminary ABMS data US copper tube production (commercial a

nd plumbing) fell by 14% in Q1 2012.  With the past expansions at Wieland Flow Products and Cerro Flow Products and modernisations elsewhere, it is highly questionable as to how much of this new capacity can readily be justified under even the most optimistic demand scenarios.  Even with anti-dumping duties in place on Chinese and Mexican sourced tube, US copper tube imports totalled 57kt in 2011 (from Canada, South Korea, China, Malaysia and Vietnam) and the bulk of these would have to be displaced to justify the new capacity.  Leading supplier Mueller Industries confirmed that it had seen lower sales volumes in its core product lines (copper tube and brass rod) and reduced margins across its operations in Q1 2012.  Mueller went on to say that, “The majority of the company’s facilities operated at significantly below capacity in 2011 and Q1 2012.” 

**A mini manufacturing revival?** The new SDI La Farga wire rod mill, coupled with the new tube mill investments, form part of a slightly brighter outlook for the downstream copper industry in the US.  Prysmian opened an extra high voltage (EHV) power cable plant in Abbeville, SC, in 2010.  ABB broke ground on its new EHV power cable plant in April 2011 in Huntersville, NC, and it is scheduled for completion by the end of 2012.  Meanwhile, Nexans announced that it is building

its own EHV power cable facility in Charleston, NC, with commissioning scheduled for 2014.  Earlier in 2012 Superior Essex Energy - part of LS Cable & System - opened its Norboro, NC, energy cable factory.  It is initially offering low voltage energy cables but it intends to become a full line supplier to the power cables market. 

### **Brazil** 

**Slower IP growth…** 2011 saw industrial growth in Brazil slow to 0.3% from 10.6% the previous year.  High real interest rates attracted strong capital inflows which led to an appreciation of the Brazilian real.  The economy has suffered the effects of a strong currency, via a loss of export competitiveness, whilst Brazilian consumers prefer cheaper imported goods over those produced domestically. 

Despite the current short term weakness, which saw Brazil’s manufacturing sector decelerate in Q1, the economy will remain fundamentally strong and demand for copper should remain robust on the back of continuing development of the economy over the next few years.  In addition to a number of government initiatives in terms of infrastructure development (many under the PAC (Growth Acceleration Program) 2 initiative), there is the football World Cup and the Olympics to prepare for, alongside continued development of oil and gas fields and offshore and onshore wind energy. Whilst Brazil will remain susceptible to outside influences, the effect of these will be much less than in the past, given the need to develop their domestic market with particular focus on infrastructure. 

**…not a reflection of

copper demand** This year, Wood Mackenzie expects that the domestic copper industry will be buoyed by recent policy announcements. Monetary stimulus began in August 2011 with the Brazilian central bank announcing a 50 basis point cut in the base interest rate.  Since then the rate has been slashed to 8.5%.  Furthermore, the government unveiled a new raft of fiscal stimulus measures worth approximately R65bn (US$32bn) on 3rd April. Domestic industry will be the main beneficiary of these tax breaks.  One key area of weakness currently is the automotive sector, where car production of 0.9M units in the first five months is 6.2% lower than the same period of 2011.  One of the tax breaks has been on lower taxes for smaller cars, whilst the central bank has also moved to increase the availability of credit for car financing.  The government has also unveiled plans that should boost infrastructure spending and have introduced taxes on imports of goods such as motorcycles and air-conditioners in a bid to support domestic producers.  The central bank is also expected to trim interest rates from the current level of 8.5% to 7.5% by the year end.  These measures are expected to stimulate the Brazilian economy in H2 2012, although given the weak state of the global economy they are unlikely to prevent a contraction in IP this year.  They will take some time before they feed into the real economy and we expect that IP will fall by -0.3% this year before growing 2.7% in 2013. 

After declining sharply by 12.7% in 2011, Brazilian copper consumption is forecast to grow by at least 3.2% to 407kt in 2012  The decline in 2011 in part reflected destocking through the downstream chain primarily during the first half of that year.  Meanwhile, the appreciating Real led to higher imports of semis from other countries in the region, which resulted in the displacement of the consumption of refined cathode across the Brazilian semi-manufacturing value chain and the decline in output of downstream products.  In 2013 and 2014, rising spending on infrastructure will help support stronger growth in refined copper consumption of 4.9% and 5.4% respectively. 

**Copper downstream sector expands…** The copper semis sector is in the hands of just a few players, including Paranapanema, Termomecanica, Cecil and Ibrame.  Paranapanema is currently the largest semis producer, with a capacity of ~100kt/a.  The company is currently on a course of downstream expansion, with the start-up of new copper tube plant in Utinga, Sao Paulo scheduled for the second half of 2012, taking capacity to 36kt/a from 18kt/a.  A new bus bar line in Sao Paulo, is due to be completed by 2013, while construction of a 200,000kt/a hot rolling mill in Sгo Mateus (ES) is scheduled for completion by 2014 following environmental approval. 

Ibrame, another fairly sizeable player, currently produces 110kt/a of copper products, aluminium products and alloys in various forms.  Ibrame have invested in a new Properzi co

pper rod mill and will produce ETP (Electrolytic Tough Pitch) copper rod using cathodes as the raw material and FRHC (Fire Refined High Conductivity) rod from copper scrap (93%94% cu content).  The project includes a refining furnace with a 100 ton capacity to process the copper scrap, a furnace set (shaft&holding) to process the copper cathodes and a CCR line with a capacity of 12.5 tph.  The plant is currently being installed and should be operational during H2 2012. 

Although the recovery in the Brazilian economy remains muted, sales of copper products have accelerated. Paranapanema’s Q1 2012 quarterly results show a 39.4% increase in year on year sales of copper rod, drawn wire and other copper products.  Sales of semis will in general continue to be affected by tough competition from imports, although the demand outlook for consumption remains positive supported by growing vehicle production and ongoing infrastructure development. **Taiwanese semis exporters diversify and remain competitive** Although Taiwanese mills have seen a 16% year-onyear slump in their export volumes to their major customers in China and Hong Kong (from 64kt to 54kt) in the first four months of 2012, they have managed to limit the overall reduction in their export sales to only 8%. **Brass mills face a tougher struggle** The Taiwanese brass mill segment is mainly focussed on the manufacture of sheet and strip and brass rod. Sheet and strip mills have endured a much more depressed and competitive market environment with existing excess capacity from Taiwan, South Korea and Japan now facing newly commissioned mills in China.
